The motion passes. All right. We've had no, no public comment. We have approved the minutes. We have no action items. And so now I will turn the floor over to Ms. Scanlon, who is going to do an introduction to the SBAC committee's roles and responsibilities.

Welcome to your very first SBAC meeting. Um, it-- o-of course, this is not, um, your first meeting because you have been doing some, um, hearings. You've done some student hearings. Uh, Ms. Labelle thought that it was very important to have a little bit of an orientation for our two new members at the beginning of our first meeting to both orient you to the policies that are under our purview, and specifically what we will

be endeavoring to do with the rest of this school year, and also to provide an orientation for you to student discipline and your role in student disciplinary appeal hearings. Of course, um, you've already gotten two of those hearings under your belt, so I think this will provide a good opportunity really to review what you've learned by experience, but it also gives you an opportunity to ask some good, thoughtful questions, I think, having already experienced the

process. Before we jump into the policies and the student discipline appeal process, I do wanna take a moment just to talk a little bit about my office. I am the director of the Office of School Administration, and we are the office that serves, um, as your liaisonum, to the leadership team and the, uh, LCPS administration. Obviously, primarily that is my role, but you will also interact with some of my staff. Certainly Ms.

Alvarado, she is here with us at the end of every month for our SBAC meetings. She is the one who puts, um, the agendas together and gets you the paperwork that you need. Uh, myself and our two hearing officers, we serve as the superintendent's designee in matters related to school discipline. Um, that is not all student discipline because only the most serious student incidents and student, um, disciplinary shank-sanctions

actually come to the attention of the superintendent's office via my office. And that is for incidents in which a student is recommended by their principal for a reassignment, an exclusion, a long-term suspension, or an expulsion. That's when my office would be involved. We conduct those hearings. We make, um, decisions on behalf of the division superintendent. And if a long-term suspension, reassignment, recommendation for

expulsion, or exclusion is appealed, that is when you all will become involved. And then, of course, our office, um, shepherds that process as well. So turning first to policy, which is one of the primary responsibilities of this committee. Um, this was our goal at the beginning of this school year. Um, I'm very happy to say we are on track towards meeting our goal.

We did already accomplish, um, the revision and passing through the full board the revisions of Policy eighty-two zero five, Student Discipline Authority, which you all actually had a part in passing because that is something that came up at the, I believe, January or early February board meeting. Um, likewise, Policy eighty-two twenty, Student Disciplinary Consequences, um, was recently

before the full board. Um, we also did earlier this school year Policy eighty-six fifty-five, Student Personal Device Use. That was decided by the full board in December so that it would be in place when the students came back after the winter holidays. And what we still have coming up are Policies eighty-two ten, currently named Introduction to Student Discipline. That policy works hand in hand with Policies eighty-two zero five and eighty-two twenty.

They're almost-- I see them as a suite of policies. So even though, um, it's not due until June, um, I actually want to do that one next because it does work hand in hand with eighty-two oh five and eighty-two twenty. Um, we are also responsible for ensuring by the end of the school year that we have revised our policy pertaining to student searches and seizure. And then finally, we have student dress code to tackle.

Um, while that policy doesn't have to be revised until mid-September, it makes sense, and Ms. Labelle pointed out, and rightly so, that if there are going to be changes to the student dress code, better that those changes are done by June so that everything can be publicized and in place for students at the beginning of the next school year. So those are the policies that we have completed, the first three, and the policies that are upcoming. Any questions on

that? Nope. Okay. Um, next then is student discipline. Um, I wanna start with just a very, very brief overview of the student discipline policy, and then we'll move into your role in that policy, which is the student disciplinary appeals process. Now, Ms. Labelle and Ms. Donahue, you would have seen portions of this presentation in August. Um, but again,

I think certainly for Mr. Stenson, who didn't have the opportunity to see some of these slides before, um, I think all of you could benefit from having an opportunity in a smaller group to ask any questions that you may wish to ask. So please, at any point, if you have questions, don't hesitate to let me know. Um, so as a brief overview, certainly we begin with what is the purpose of student discipline to begin with. Um, of course, primary purpose, certainly at

our level of discipline, is student safety. Uh, promoting safe learning environments where our students can come to school and not only be safe, but feel safe. And the same goes for our staff. Um, obviously we want our staff as well to be able to feel that they can come to work and both be safe and feel safe. Um, promoting student discipline, especially at the school level, again, we see the most, um, severe outcomes or the most serious offenses.

Uh, most, the by far most discipline is handled at the school level, and that really is done in an effort to promote the instructional program. Safety is a piece of that, but in general, we also need to ensure that our students are learning in an environment that is actually conducive to learning, um, with as little disruption as possible to that instructional program. The discipline process also can serve to engage both students and parents in, um,

understanding the need to help a student resolve certain behavioral issues before, um, they are facing more stringent consequences that take them out of the instructional program. For example, um, through suspensions or in the worst case scenario, um, an appearance before my office or before you. And then of course, there are certain disciplinary actions that have to be made in accordance with federal law, state law, and certain

policies and regulations, um, that require certain sanctions.So very briefly, um, the process for student discipline always begins with some kind of allegation. Allegations come to our school administrators in a variety of ways. Oftentimes it comes from students making allegations.

Those students can be victims or targets. They can be witnesses. They can be students who just have a concern and they come forward with an allegation. School officials receive allegations as well from parents, from community members, from staff members, etc. Whenever there is an allegation of student misconduct, um, that occurs within the school system's jurisdiction, then the school administrator will launch an investigation. The investigation, the goal of

that is to determine whether or not the misconduct actually occurred. Um, our school administrators cannot make a determination that, uh, misconduct occurred without actually doing the investigation to demonstrate that that was the case. In the course of their investigation, they're collecting primarily student statements. Um, student witness reports are the most common piece of evidence they receive.

That might be supplemented with documentary evidence, um, such as video. Sometimes c- our cameras or a student's camera captures incidents. In that case, video will be reviewed. There might be physical e-evidence in the forms of contraband that was, um, seized or discovered in the course of an investigation. There might be photos of physical injury. There might be photos of damage to personal property or

LCPS property, etc. But via that investigation, they're collecting all of that information, and then they have to determine based on a preponderance of the evidence that the student, more likely than not, being the preponderance, is responsible for the alleged misconduct in order to determine that yes, in fact, the student has violated our, our policies and our code of conduct. If they determine there was a violation, then they use a

tool that is provided for them. Um, it's a system-wide tool. It's known colloquially as the SBAR. People call it the SBAR tool. Um, that's a little bit misnamed, so I intend to rebrand it in our next policy. But essentially, it takes ninety-four different violations. They have to determine of that list of ninety-four which occurred. It may be that only one violation occurred.

It may be that the student committed multiple violations on that list. And then as they come across the tool, they will see what their range of permissible sanction is for the violation that occurred. So they do their investigation. They de-- If they determine that, uh, misconduct occurred, they label that misconduct, and they l- use this tool to determine their range of sanction. They then choose the sanction. They have to be within their range

based on the seriousness of what occurred, the impact of what occurred, and any other prior disciplinary, um, events that may have occurred from a progressive standpoint. They can factor that in as well. They administer that sanction, and most sanctions, um, that occur at the school level, which you'll see in just a moment, anything less than a suspension from school is not appealable. If the student is

suspended from school, at that point, a family could appeal to my office, and if it is simply a short-term suspension, which is a suspension anywhere from one to ten days, then we are the final arbiter of that suspension. If we get a case with a ten-day suspension and a referral to our office from so- for some additional action, then that is

when you all may be involved in an appeal, and that becomes then an appeal of our decision rather than the principal's decision. So this is data related to the twenty-four-twenty-five school year. You can see here, if we added all of that up, we have approximately twenty-three thousand, uh, sanctions that were administered last school year.

Now, there can be overlap. A student can receive multiple sanctions for the same, um, violation. So there were approximately nineteen thousand incidents recorded in our Phoenix, our, our student information system, and those nineteen thousand incidents resulted in approximately, um, twenty-three thousand sanctions. What I wanted you to take away from this, however, is that the vast majority of

sanctions could never appe- appear before this board. The only sanctions that are appealable to SBAC are the three that you see at the very end or the far right of that screen. Um, one hundred and twelve reassignment decisions, any one of those could be appealed to SBAC. Fourteen long-term suspension decisions, and then in the last school year, we had no expulsion recommendations. But that is the universe of what you

might be involved in. But in order to be involved in those sanctions, a parent would actually have to appeal our decision that those sanctions be implemented. So this shows you a three-year perspective. Um, actually, it's more of a, a two-and-a-half year perspective because we're only partway through twenty-five-twenty-six, but of the number of

appeals that SBAC has heard. So you will seeUm, for example, that there's a difference between an appeal being filed and an appeal being heard. So I'm gonna discuss that. That, that's one big takeaway there, and that you will see in that middle, um, cluster of columns. In addition, what you will see is that

even when you consider not, not only the, the 19,000 sanctions that were administered, but within what was potentially in your realm, you had about 160 that could have come to you. The numbers that actually do come to you on appeal are really quite low. Um, last year, '24-'25, there were 19 appeals filed, and there were

el-11 appeals heard. So there were 11 SBAC hearings conducted last school year. So you might be saying, "Well, why would, uh, something be appealed but then not heard?" There were eight cases that were appealed, um, but not heard. Of those eight, two, the parent withdrew. The parent decided, "You know, now that I've had more time to think about this," they might have had some questions that were answered. They've decided they didn't want to move forward with

the appeal, which is fine. Um, they do have to notify me of that in writing so that there's no question of their intent. And if they notify me in writing that they wish not to appeal, as long as I have that before, uh, the day of the appeal, then we would just go ahead and cancel the hearing, and our decision would stand. The other six, um, were all instances of community-based crimes, where

between our reassignment decision and the time that SBAC would have convened, the court acted and either dismissed the charges or diminished the charges to a point that our decision had to be, um, rescinded in any case. So essentially, the appeal became moot before it was ever heard by SBAC. And if it's moot, then there's no reason to go forward with the appeal hearing. Any questions on

that? I can see it in your face, Ms. Donahue. That's why I paused. Thank you, Chair LaBelle. Uh, and thank you, Ms. Scanlon. Um, so I, I just want to ask for some clarification or for you to help me talk through, um, kinda the last point that you made. So, uh, on the one hand, I hear what you're saying, but on the other hand,

our discipline process is separate from criminal process. So when you say a court procedure might make our appeal moot, can you explain what you mean by that? Yes, that's a very good question. Um, in the vast majority of situations, our discipline process is absolutely and completely separate from a court process.

Okay? And in fact, the two hearings that you've participated in so far, that was absolutely the case. So those are situations, and I would say when you think about all of the cases we get in my office, I would say probably 90% of the cases that are sent to us are cases where whatever happened, happened fully and totally within our jurisdiction. So it happened on school property, at a school-sponsored activity, uh, with the use of our

devices or our networks, something that was fully within our jurisdiction. We have the independent authority and responsibility to act, and that authority and that responsibility exists regardless of what the court might do. Whether there are charges, whether charges, um, continue forward through a pro-court process, whether there's a conviction, not a conviction, doesn't matter to the student discipline process because we have an independent

authority. We also, under the Code of Virginia, can take action against a student who has been charged with or convicted of certain serious community-based offenses. It is not most offenses. Um, the vast majority of offenses for which students are criminally charged would never come to the attention of the division superintendent.

But the code sets forth 14 categories of criminal offenses such that if a juvenile is charged with one of those 14 categories of offenses, then the intake officer at the Juvenile and Domestic Relations District Court must notify the superintendent. Those charges come, um, to me as the superintendent's designee. Um, I will send those charges out to

the principals as ordained by law and policy, and then the principals can determine whether or not, based on that charge alone, um, the principal feels it would be prudent to have the student reassigned. So these are instances where a student has been charged with community-based offense. They did not occur on school property, at a school-sponsored activity, via our devices, our technologies.

They are entirely outside of the independent realm of our jurisdiction. They are the most serious charges. Um, the 14 categories include, um, murder, other fo-felonious assaults, including sexual assaults, uh, gang activity, gang recruitment, burglary, arson, um, robbery, certain weapons offenses, but not

most, certain drug offenses, but not most. So they are very serious offenses.If we reassign a student or take any disciplinary action based on a charge alone, um, then because our authority rests solely on that community-based charge, if the community-based charge goes away or is reduced to a charge that isn't on the list of

fourteen, then our th-authority to take that action goes away with it. So in those six cases, we had a student charged with a reportable offense. We enacted a reassignment. The family appealed the reassignment, but before we got to the SBAC appeal, they had gone to court, and either the charge was completely dismissed, they were found not guilty of the charge, or the charge was reduced such that it was no longer on

the list of fourteen, which means I had to rescind the decision. I did rescind the decision, rendering the appeal moot. That's very helpful. Thank you, Ms. Gitlin. You're welcome. Okay, um, appeals to SBAC, um, and the pr-the process is entirely laid out in Policy eighty-two thirty, which was updated about a year

ago, um, approximately a year, year ago. I think it's very thorough, um, but it does set forth all of these items and more. Um, regarding the scope of SBAC authority, this is important. Um, SBAC has the authority to affirm, modify, or annul a sanction decision. SBAC doesn't have the authority to

adjust the finding that the student violated the rules, but SBAC has the authority to determine whether the sanction that was administered for that violation was the appropriate sanction. Only certain sanctions, as we mentioned before, are appealable to SBAC. Um, the vast majority of sanctions aren't. In order to appear before SBAC, a

student must have been either long-term suspended, which is a suspension of between eleven days and three hundred and sixty-four days, or they must have been reassigned from the school in which they were enrolled to a different setting, a reassignment decision, or they would have had to have been excluded, which is a process, um, that is dependent or is specifically for a

student who has gotten long-term suspended or expelled someplace else, and then in the term of that expulsion or long, or long-term suspension, have tried to enroll here. If we then excluded the student based on the disciplinary action that was taken by the other school division or private school, an exclusion could also be appealed. So long-term suspension, reassignment, exclusion, or a

recommendation for expulsion. Now, a recommendation for expulsion is interesting because it's the only one that has to go to SBAC, whether there is an appeal or not, and that is simply because while the superintendent can recommend expulsion, the superintendent doesn't have the authority to expel. Only you have the authority to expel. So if there is a recommendation for expulsion, it's essentially, um, my hearing officer acting on behalf of the superintendent has opened a circle that has

to be closed, and only SBAC can close that circle. So, uh, expulsion recommendations have to come to you, whether or not appealed. Long-term suspensions, reassignments, and exclusion decisions would come to you only if appealed. Appeal packets, um, you are familiar now with what an appeal packet looks like. Um, it is the entire record that was before the hearing officer. In addition to the hearing

officer's decision, the appeal submitted by the parent, um, and that's essentially it. So it's the record that was before us, plus our decision, plus the parent's appeal that goes to the SBAC members, and a copy of that in redacted form also goes to the family. In terms of the hearing itself, um, both sides, so to speak, the family has an opportunity to present its version of events

and its arguments for why a decision should be modified or overturned. The school administration, um, represented by the hearing officer, has the ability to do the same. Um, there are closing arguments on each side. Um, certainly SBAC has the, um, the fortune of having, um, division counsel sit in if there are any legal questions that you may have. Families also have the ability to be represented at these hearings,

um, by whomever they wish to bring with them as a support. That could be an attorney. Uh, that could be a family member. That could be really anyone that they wish to bring with them. Um, so that hearing gives an opportunity for SBAC to hear both perspectives of what occurred, both perspectives regarding what should happen next in terms of a sanction, and it gives an opportunity as well

for you to make sure that your questions are answered so that you can make the best possible decision regarding what should happen next for that student. You do deliberate completely. Um, the, the entire hearing, as you know, is in closed session, but your deliberation is private. It is the three of you with division counsel in the event you have legal questions. You are the only ones that are privy to that deliberation, and your decision is to either

affirm the hearing officer's decision, annul the hearing officer's decision, or modify it, and that modification, um, could take any form that you like.Once SBAC makes a decision, so long as that decision is unanimous, it is the final decision, and it is unappealable. If SBAC makes a decision that is not unanimous, so a two-to-one decision, then the family could

appeal that non-unanimous decision to the full school board, and the full school board would hear that, um, that case, or they would receive that case. They wouldn't really hear it in the sense that that appeal would typically be on the written record. So there wouldn't be an additional hearing. All of the paperwork, the record, would then go to the full board, supplemented only with the SBAC decision

and then the family's appeal of the SBAC decision. That packet would go to each member of the full board, and that appeal would be done on the written record in a closed meeting of the full board. Um, at that point, that is the final word, and again, it only reaches the full board if it, it, there is a non-unanimous decision at your level. Okay. That may be... Oh, no, I was gonna say that may be my last slide, but no, it isn't.

This is a very important one, and Ms. Labelle said, "You need to make sure you talk about this." Um, and she was right. This will often come up in hearings, um, where we have a student who has a disability and either has an IEP or a 504 plan. Um, so you should know that students with disabilities who have either a 504 or an IEP do have

additional protections in the discipline process. Um, the first protection is a manifestation determination review where a, uh, relevant members of the student's IEP team must convene. They, um, are expected to convene before the tenth day of suspension, and they are tasked with reviewing the incident, reviewing what is known of the student's disability,

and answering r-really two questions. Uh, question one is, "Was the student's misconduct a direct result of the student's disability?" And/or question two, "Was the student's misconduct a direct result of the school system's failure to implement the IEP or the 504 plan with fidelity?" So

those relevant members of the IEP team, which do include the parents, um, and in some cases, even the student if the student is old enough to participate, they go through the incident, they go through the student's disability, and they answer each of those two questions. If the answer to both questions is no, no, the misconduct was neither a result, a direct result of the student's disability nor a direct result of any failure of the division to implement the IEP,

then two no's equals not a manifestation of the student's disability. If either of the two questions gets a yes, then that is equal to the misconduct is a manifestation of the student's disability. The reason that is important is, under IDEA and our own policy, any student where it is determined that their misconduct was a manifestation of their disability

cannot be disciplined beyond a cumulative, for the entire school year, ten days of suspension. So we do occasionally have situations where a referral is sent to my office because of serious misconduct. Um, the MDR is done, and typically, the MDR would be done before my office conducts a hearing. If the determination is that it's a manifestation, often what you will see is we cancel the

hearing, um, and we do not move forward with any kind of, um, involvement. Um, the student sanction ends on the tenth cumulative day of suspension, and the matter goes back to an IEP team to do a, um, FBA, a BIP, and to figure out what accommodations need to be in place to ensure that serious misconduct does not recur. For a matter to come to SBAC, it

can, by definition, only come to you if the determination was that the student's misconduct was not a direct manifestation of their disability, and that is because if it is a manifestation, we cannot long-term suspend, reassign, exclude, or recommend expulsion. So by virtue of the fact that we have made that decision, it has been determined by the IEP team or relevant members thereof that

the student's misconduct is not what directly led or, or was not directly caused by the disability. Sometimes what you will see in hearings is, in part or in whole, the appeal is really based on the special education matters where a parent may argue to you, or family may argue to you, that because of the student's

disability, um, the sanction should not have occurred, or the misconduct occurred because of the student's disability. And what-- But that matter has already been resolved through the MDR process. So when that occurs, what, what you will often hear me say, as I'm sitting over here, is that the parent does have the right and the ability to appeal the MDR decision-It's a separate

process. So when there is an appeal of the MDR decision, that goes to a due process hearing officer. There is a hearing that is done to determine whether or not that MDR should be overturned. If the MDR is overturned, I would get notice of that, and I would have to rescind the decision based on, um, the MDR being overturned on appeal. But what, what cannot happen or should not happen

is for SBAC to make those special education decisions. Um, so often when we're here, it's, it's really a lot of education, I think, um, in ensuring that parents understand that they do have an avenue for appealing special education determinations. Um, but that avenue is separate from the student discipline avenue.

And in the red box, you see, uh, the important documents that set forth the various rights of students with disabilities. Regulation, uh, eighty two twenty point three sets forth, um, from an LCPS perspective what additional, um, processes and protections our students with disabilities have. And then, of course, um, there are two other documents that parents are provided through the special education processes: the Virginia Procedural Safeguards Notice and, um, for students with
